text: My life came to an unexpected standstill. I could breathe, eat, drink, and sleep, and I could not help doing so; but there was no authentic life, because I had no desires the fulfillment of which I could consider reasonable. If a fairy had come and offered to fulfill any desire I had, I would not have known what to ask. The truth was that life appeared utterly meaningless. I had lived and walked until I had arrived at a precipice, and saw clearly that there was nothing ahead of me but destruction. Neither art nor literature nor wealth could answer the gnawing question: 'Why should I live, why should I do anything?'

chapter: Chapter 4: The Dragon and the Drops of Honey
text: There is an ancient fable about a traveler overtaken in a plain by a raging beast. Seeking safety, he leaps into a dry well, but at the bottom sees a dragon with open jaws waiting to devour him. Clinging to the twigs of a wild bush growing from the stone wall, his hands grow weak. Two mice, one white and one black, circle the bush and steadily gnaw through its stem. Yet the traveler sees drops of honey upon the leaves, and stretches out his tongue to lick them. Thus do men cling to the bush of life, knowing the dragon of death waits below, while day and night gnaw away at our existence; and the petty pleasures of art and family no longer console us once the reality of death is unmasked.

chapter: Chapter 9: The Faith of the Simple People
text: I turned away from the rich, the learned, and the idle, and began to observe the life of the simple working people. I saw millions of peasants who endured harsh labor, sickness, and poverty with quiet tranquility and joy, because they possessed an unshakeable faith in the meaning of life. I realized that pure rational knowledge cannot give life meaning; rationality leads only to despair and the void. Faith alone connects the finite human being with the infinite universe. To live as a human being, one must possess faith—not dogmatic ritual, but the inner living realization of love and moral duty.

chapter: Chapter 12: To Know God is to Live
text: I remember walking in the woods in early spring. The moment I lost awareness of God, life died within me, and cold despair seized my heart. But the instant I turned my soul toward God, life returned in all its fullness. 'What more do you seek?' a voice cried within me. 'He is that without which one cannot live. To know God and to live is one and the same thing. God is life.' Live seeking God, love your neighbor, perform honest work, and despair will vanish like mist before the sun.

chapter: Chapter 7: The Falsity of Conventional Life
text: What tormented Ivan Ilyich most on his deathbed was the deception and the lie: that he was merely sick and not dying, and that he need only remain quiet and obey the physicians. This conventional falsity, which everyone maintained around him and within him, did more than physical pain to poison his dying days. He looked back upon his legal career, his comfortable bourgeois furniture, his social triumphs, and his respectable decorum, and recognized with horror that his entire adulthood had been a gigantic, artificial falsehood that veiled the reality of the soul.

chapter: Chapter 12: The Light that Conquers Death
text: In his final agony, Ivan Ilyich looked at his weeping schoolboy son, who kissed his hand, and he felt profound pity and love. His lifelong egotism and terror suddenly fell away. 'How good and how simple!' he thought. 'And death? Where is it?' He sought his former accustomed fear of death and did not find it. 'Where is it? What death?' There was no fear because there was no death. In place of death there was light. 'So that is it!' he exclaimed aloud. 'What joy!' He drew in his breath, stopped in the midst of a sigh, stretched out, and died in peace.

The privileged intellectuals of my class attempt to escape the problem of existence in four ways: blind ignorance, hedonistic distraction, suicide through violent despair, or weak, cowardly compliance. Yet none of these solves the riddle. The true answer is found in renouncing selfish egoism, serving our fellow human beings through daily physical labor, and surrendering our intellect to the infinite compassion and moral law of God.
